vignette:
Carlos is a fifty-three-year-old tax consultant who was pulled over by police during a routine traffic stop in his own neighborhood two years ago. What began as a minor infraction escalated within seconds: the officer drew his weapon, ordered Carlos to the ground, and pinned him face-down on the asphalt with a knee pressed into his lower back. Carlos heard his own ribs crack. He lay there, gasping, while the officer shouted commands he could barely process. Another cruiser arrived; the second officer stood over him, radioing in his license plate. Carlos remembers the weight of the knee, the gravel cutting into his cheek, and the sound of his own voice—thin, pleading, unrecognizable—saying he was sorry, though he did not know for what. He was released with a warning and a citation for a broken taillight. No charges were filed. But the damage was done.

In the weeks that followed, Carlos began to notice that his body remembered things his mind tried to push away. Whenever he saw someone with a visible injury—a bruise, a bandage, a cast—his chest would tighten and his thoughts would spiral. He started to believe that there was something about him, something intrinsic and unchangeable, that had made the event happen. He had always been a careful man, a rule-follower, but now he felt fundamentally marked. At a client meeting, a junior associate mentioned a news story about police violence, and Carlos excused himself to the restroom, his hands trembling. He stood in the stall, gripping the sink, and thought: I am not the same person anymore. I don't know who I am. The memory of the officer's face, indifferent and unmoved, returned to him unbidden. He began to feel isolated from his colleagues, from his ex-wife, from the life he had built. He told himself he did not deserve to feel safe.

These appraisals fed a growing vigilance. Carlos started to avoid unfamiliar places entirely—new restaurants, different routes to work, even the grocery store on the other side of town—because he could not assess the danger. He began to look behind him constantly, checking for anyone who might be following. At his desk, he would find himself scanning the parking lot through the blinds, mapping escape routes before he could settle into his chair. The world had become a threat surface, and he was responsible for reading it. What frightened him most was the thought that if he let his guard down for even a moment, something terrible would happen again—and this time, it would be his fault. The vigilance, in turn, deepened his belief that he was broken. He would catch himself scanning a coffee shop for exits and think: Normal people do not do this. There is something wrong with me. The more he watched for danger, the more convinced he became that danger was everywhere, and that he was the only one who saw it.

The cycle tightened. His hypervigilance made him more alert to potential triggers: the sight of a police cruiser in his rearview mirror, the sound of a raised voice in a hallway, the sudden pressure of a hand on his shoulder. Each trigger reactivated the memory of the knee in his back, and each reactivation reinforced his belief that he was fundamentally at fault. He began to experience sharp, stabbing pain in his lower back—the same spot where the officer had knelt—even when he had done nothing to aggravate it. The pain became a trigger in itself, a physical reminder that his body was still telling the story. He started to wonder whether his life was worth living anymore. He did not share this thought with anyone.

Carlos finally came to therapy at the urging of his daughter, who had noticed he was no longer attending family dinners or returning her calls. He sat in the waiting room with his back to the wall, having already identified the nearest exit. When the therapist asked what he hoped to gain from treatment, Carlos hesitated. He said he wanted to stop being afraid. Then, quieter, he said he wanted to stop believing that what happened was his fault.
